I will report back once the next term's figures are in.

Yours sincerely,
[Name]

I'm home on Tuesday and Thursday afternoons, so a plumber would be welcome to come at either of those times.

Please let me know what can be arranged.

Hi team,

Here's a quick update on the online ordering test we ran from 6 to 19 October. Half of our website visitors were shown the new one-page order form, and the other half saw the old three-step form.

The new form received 212 orders from 3,050 visits (roughly 7.0%), while the old form received 198 orders from 3,010 visits (roughly 6.6%). The new form's rate is a touch higher, but Tomas Reyes, our web developer, has looked at the numbers and says the gap is too small to tell apart from chance. In short, the test is inconclusive so far, and we can't yet say one form outperforms the other.

We'll keep collecting data and share more once the picture is clearer.

Thanks

Dear Mrs Adeyemi,

I wanted to give you a brief update on the paired reading programme we ran in Year 4 over the past 8 weeks. All 26 pupils in the class took part. On the end of term reading test, the group's average reading age was up by 5 months compared with the start of term.

I do want to be careful about how we read that figure. There was no comparison class, the same teacher marked both the baseline and the end of term tests, and children at this age often make gains of a similar size over a single term. So while the result is encouraging, we cannot yet attribute the improvement to the programme itself.

The literacy lead has suggested we run the programme for a further term before considering a school-wide recommendation, so we will collect another full set of data before drawing firmer conclusions.

I am happy to go through the details with you at your convenience.

Yours sincerely,
[Name]

**Note to the Rosemary Lane Bakery Team**

**Re: Online Ordering Form Test, 6 to 19 October**

During the two-week test, we split website visitors into two groups. One group (3,050 visits) saw the new one-page order form, and the other (3,010 visits) continued to see the old three-step form.

**Results:**

- New one-page form: 212 orders (a 6.9% conversion rate)
- Old three-step form: 198 orders (a 6.6% conversion rate)

The new form produced a slightly higher number of orders, but Tomas Reyes, our web developer, has reviewed the figures and confirmed that the gap is within the range of normal variation. In other words, we cannot yet say with confidence that one form outperforms the other.

**Bottom line:** The test is inconclusive at this stage. We do not have enough evidence to declare a winner, and we should avoid treating the small uptick in the new form's numbers as a proven improvement.

**Next steps:** We will keep the test running to gather more visits before making a decision on which form to keep. I will share an update once we have a larger sample.

If you have any questions about the numbers or the methodology, please reach out.

Thanks,
[Your name]

Best,
[Your name]

Note to Mrs Adeyemi

Re: Paired Reading Programme, Year 4

I wanted to give you a brief summary of the 8-week paired reading trial we ran with a group of 26 Year 4 pupils.

On the end-of-term reading test, the group's average reading age rose by 5 months compared with their start-of-term score. That is a positive figure, and the children have responded well to the sessions in practice.

I do want to flag a few caveats before we read too much into the number:

- There was no comparison class, so we cannot isolate the effect of the programme from general term-time progress.
- The same teacher marked both the pre- and post-tests, which introduces the possibility of marker drift.
- Children at this age routinely make gains of a similar size over a single term, so the 5-month rise is within what we might expect even without the intervention.

In short, the result is encouraging but not yet conclusive evidence of a causal effect.

Our literacy lead has asked for a further term of data, ideally with a matched comparison group and independent marking, before making a recommendation to roll the programme out school-wide. I am happy to plan that follow-up in the next term and will report back with the fuller picture.

Please let me know if you would like me to go into more detail on any of the above.

Kind regards,
[Name]
[Role]

Here's a quick update on the online ordering test we ran on the website from 6 to 19 October.

During that period we split our website visitors into two groups. Half were shown a new one-page order form, and half were shown the old three-step form.

That means the test is inconclusive so far. It does not yet tell us whether the new form is better, worse, or the same as the old one, so we are not making any changes on the strength of this result. We'll keep the data and revisit the test before drawing any conclusions.

Thanks,
[Your name]

I wanted to pass on a quick summary of how our autumn author events went. Between 3 September and 22 October we ran five events in total, and the turnout was a real pleasure to see. Thanks to everyone who helped set up, restock, and keep the kettle running. It was a great season for the shop, and I think we've built a nice rhythm that's worth carrying into the winter.

Warmly,
The Events Team

Between 1 March and 31 August, 3,500 households in the Oakmere ward took part in a trial of weekly food waste collections using a small kitchen caddy.

During the same period, general rubbish in Oakmere fell by 6 percent compared with the equivalent months last year. Across the whole borough, general rubbish fell by 3 percent over that period. So far, 52 percent of trial households reported using the caddy regularly.

Kind regards

reply:
**Food Waste Caddy Trial: Update for Council Members**

**Trial overview**
Between 1 March and 31 August, 3,500 households in the Oakmere ward took part in a food waste caddy trial. Participants received a small kitchen caddy and had weekly food waste collections for the duration of the six-month period.

**Results so far**
During the trial months, general rubbish collected in Oakmere fell by 6 per cent compared with the same months last year. Over the same period, general rubbish across the whole borough fell by 3 per cent. While Oakmere's reduction was larger than the borough-wide figure, it is not yet possible to attribute the full 6 per cent drop solely to the caddy scheme, as other factors (for example, seasonal variation or parallel waste-reduction messaging) may also have played a part.

**Uptake**
Only 52 per cent of trial households reported using the caddy regularly. This suggests that a meaningful share of participants either used it sporadically or not at all, which limits the scale of the effect observed.

**Landfill impact**
Our recycling officer, Dan Whitlock, has noted that the effect on landfill volumes is not yet clear. Further analysis is needed to determine whether the food waste diverted through the caddy has measurably reduced the amount sent to landfill, or whether it has simply shifted material into another part of the waste stream.

**Next steps**
We will continue to monitor uptake and waste tonnages through the autumn and will bring a fuller assessment, including landfill data, to a future council meeting.

If you have questions or would like the underlying data, please contact the Waste Services team.

**Update for Wexley Council Members: Food Waste Caddy Trial, Oakmere Ward**

From 1 March to 31 August, 3,500 households in the Oakmere ward took part in a trial of weekly food waste collections using a small kitchen caddy.

**Results so far**

- General rubbish in Oakmere fell by 6 percent over the trial period, compared with the same months last year.
- Across the whole borough, general rubbish fell by 3 percent over the same period.
- Because the borough-wide reduction was 3 percent, the trial's specific contribution to Oakmere's 6 percent drop is, at most, 3 percentage points. A direct causal link has not yet been established.
- Only 52 percent of the 3,500 trial households reported using the caddy regularly, so uptake was limited.

**Landfill impact**

Our recycling officer, Dan Whitlock, has noted that the effect of the trial on landfill volumes is not yet clear and that further data is needed before a firm conclusion can be drawn.

**Next steps**

We will continue to monitor usage and waste volumes over the coming months. A fuller evaluation, including a review of whether the caddy model is worth extending to other wards, will be presented to Council at a future meeting.

Please direct any questions to the Waste Services team.

During that window, new users were split at random into two groups. Half saw the new interactive tutorial, and half saw the old welcome screens. In total, 4,800 new users took part.

Results:
- Day-7 retention with the tutorial: 34.1%
- Day-7 retention with the old welcome screens: 33.4%

That is a difference of 0.7 percentage points in favor of the tutorial. At this point we cannot say the tutorial has a meaningful effect on day-7 retention.

Recommendation: hold off on any decision to roll out or drop the tutorial based on this round alone. If the team wants a clearer answer, we would need a larger sample or a longer test window to narrow the margin of error.

Happy to walk through the details if useful.

Thanks

Allowance figures for part-time staff are still being checked.

If you have any questions in the meantime, please don't hesitate to reach out.

Thanks,
[Name]

We will keep monitoring and may run a follow-up test to get a clearer read.

Thanks

The early numbers are encouraging but limited by the wet-weather disruption. We will return to governors with the full-term data before drawing any firm conclusions.

Since 1 February, 2,000 homes in the Kilbride area have been enrolled in the smart meter leak alert pilot. Residents receive a text message when their meter registers continuous flow overnight, which can indicate a slow leak or a running toilet.

Network engineer Aoife Byrne cautions that it is not yet possible to attribute the 4 percent reduction to the alerts alone, as other factors (including the Kilbride Road main repair) may account for part of the change. The pilot will continue, and further analysis is planned once a longer data set is available.

Since 1 February, 2,000 homes in the Kilbride area have been enrolled in the smart meter leak alert pilot. When a meter detects continuous flow overnight, the household receives a text message prompting them to check for a leak.

**Results to date (first four months):**

- 37 leaks were reported by residents and subsequently fixed.
- Estimated water loss in the Kilbride area fell by 4 percent over the period.
- A burst main on Kilbride Road was identified and repaired in March.

**Caveat:** Network engineer Aoife Byrne has noted that it is not yet possible to attribute the 4 percent reduction in water loss specifically to the alert pilot. Other factors, including the Kilbride Road main repair and general network maintenance, may have contributed. Further monitoring will be needed to isolate the pilot's effect.

We will continue to track alert volumes, response times, and area-level loss data before drawing firmer conclusions on the scheme's impact.

From 1 October to 30 November, a seaweed-based feed additive was trialled on 60 cows in the east shed, while a further 60 cows in the west shed continued on the standard ration as a control group.

Over the eight-week period, average daily milk yield in the east shed was 29.6 litres per cow, compared with 28.9 litres in the west shed.

However, as our vet Siobhan Healy has pointed out, the east shed housed a higher proportion of cows in early lactation during the trial window. **Smart Meter Leak Alert Pilot – Kilbride Area: Four-Month Update**

Since 1 February, 2,000 homes in the Kilbride area have been enrolled in the smart meter leak alert pilot. When a meter registers continuous flow overnight, the household receives a text message prompting them to check for a possible leak.

Over the first four months of the trial, 37 leaks were reported and subsequently repaired. Estimated water loss across the area fell by 4 percent during the same period. A burst main on Kilbride Road was also repaired in March, which is a separate infrastructure issue from the meter alerts.

Network engineer Aoife Byrne has noted that it is not yet possible to attribute a specific portion of the 4 percent reduction to the alert system alone. The fall in water loss may reflect a combination of the pilot, the Kilbride Road repair, seasonal variation, and other factors. Further monitoring will be needed before a clearer picture of the pilot's individual contribution emerges.

In short, the pilot is running as designed and has supported the identification and repair of a meaningful number of leaks, but the evidence so far does not yet isolate its direct impact on overall water loss.

For the spring appeal we split our 800 supporters into two equal groups of 400. One group received the email with the long standing subject line; the other received the new one. The new subject line produced a 31 percent open rate, compared with 27 percent for the old one.

Our volunteer statistician, Owen, has looked at the figures and notes that a four percentage point gap with 400 people in each group is within the range we would expect from random variation alone. In other words, we cannot yet say the new subject line is genuinely better; the result is suggestive but not conclusive.

We will repeat the test with the autumn appeal, using the same split and the same two subject lines, so that we have a second, independent data point before deciding which line to keep. If the autumn results point the same way, our confidence will be considerably stronger. If they do not, we will treat the spring difference as a chance fluctuation.

Weekday cycle trips rose from an average of 310 a day to 365 a day. However, two factors make it difficult to read too much into this figure. Council Transport Team

**Gatley Road Protected Bike Lane Pilot: Early Update**

A temporary protected bike lane was installed on Gatley Road on 1 April. Cycle traffic counts were taken in June, and the results are now available.

**What the counts show**

Weekday cycle trips rose from an average of 310 per day to 365 per day. That is an increase of 55 trips a day, or roughly 18 per cent.

**Important context**

Two factors make it difficult to attribute this rise to the lane itself:

- The traffic counter was relocated 50 metres during the installation, so the two sets of counts were not taken from the same position.
- June weather was unusually dry, which tends to encourage more cycling than a wetter month would.

**What the council says**

Gareth Lyle, the council's transport officer, notes that it is too early to say whether the lane itself increased cycling. The council will continue to monitor the route and will share further findings as more data is gathered.

We will keep residents informed as the pilot progresses. If you have any questions, please contact the council's transport team.

Yours sincerely,
Gatley Road Neighbourhood Team

Here's a quick update on the pilot test of the new anti corrosion coating.

We coated 3 steel test panels and exposed them in the salt spray chamber for 500 hours, comparing them against uncoated control panels. Two of the three coated panels showed less corrosion than the controls. The third coated panel showed no difference from its control, and we do not yet have an explanation for that result.

With only three panels, this is too small a sample to draw firm conclusions, so we should treat this as a preliminary signal rather than a confirmed result. The full test, using 24 panels and a 2000 hour exposure, is scheduled to start in March, and that will give us a much stronger basis to judge whether the coating performs reliably.

Our next steps are to investigate the third panel to understand why it did not perform the same as the other two, and to confirm that the full test is on track for March.

Best regards

**Subject: Spring Appeal Subject Line Test – Results**

Dear Trustees,

During the spring appeal we ran a small test comparing two email subject lines. Of our 800 supporters, 400 received the old subject line and 400 received a new one. The new subject line produced a 31 percent open rate compared with 27 percent for the old, a difference of four percentage points.

Our volunteer statistician, Owen, has pointed out that with only 400 recipients in each group, a gap of this size could plausibly be due to chance rather than a genuine difference between the two lines. In short, the result is encouraging but not yet conclusive; we cannot confidently say the new subject line outperforms the old.

We plan to repeat the test with the autumn appeal. If the new subject line shows a similar or larger advantage again, we will have stronger grounds to adopt it as our standard. We will report back once those figures are in.

Yours sincerely,
[Name]

reply:
**Self-Checkout Kiosk Pilot: March Update**

Hi everyone,

Thanks to all the volunteers who helped with the self-checkout kiosk pilot. The two kiosks were in use from 3 March to 28 March, and staff recorded 1,140 kiosk loans over that period.

On the queue side, the average Saturday wait at the main desk dropped from 9 minutes to 7 minutes. That is a welcome change, but it is worth noting that this year's school holidays shifted to April, so fewer families were in the building during March. Because of that, we cannot yet say the kiosks were responsible for the shorter wait.

Branch manager Ines Okafor has asked that we collect another month of data before making any decision about keeping, expanding, or removing the kiosks. If you are available in April, your help with Friday and Saturday shifts would be especially useful.

We will share the full April figures once they are in. In the meantime, please keep an eye on the kiosks and flag any issues to the front desk.

Thanks again for your support.

The Brookfield Library Team

Coldharbour Farm – Cover Crop Trial, First Season

Last autumn we sowed crimson clover on the 14-hectare north field and left the 12-hectare east field bare over the winter. This summer the north field produced 8.1 tonnes of wheat per hectare and the east field 7.8, a difference of 0.3 t/ha in favour of the clover field.

Priya Nair, our agronomist, cautions against reading too much into that gap. The north field has better drainage to begin with, so part of the yield difference may simply reflect soil conditions rather than the clover. She also notes that a single season is not enough to draw a conclusion. At this stage we cannot say whether the crimson clover made any meaningful difference to the wheat crop.

We will continue the trial next season, keeping the same two fields under the same treatment, so that we can compare a second year's data. We will report back once we have that fuller picture.

Dear Partners,

A quick update on the cover crop trial we ran last year. In autumn, we sowed crimson clover across the 14-hectare north field and left the 12-hectare east field bare over the winter. This summer the north field produced 8.1 tonnes of wheat per hectare, compared with 7.8 in the east field.

That said, we would not want to read too much into the 0.3-tonne gap. Priya Nair, our agronomist, has flagged two important caveats. First, the north field has better drainage to begin with, so part of the difference may simply reflect the ground itself rather than the clover. Second, one season is far too short a window to draw any firm conclusion about the effect of a cover crop on the following cereal.

In short, the trial is a useful first data point, but it is not yet clear whether the crimson clover made any meaningful difference to the wheat yield. We will continue monitoring both fields over the coming seasons before deciding on a wider rollout.

Best regards,
The Coldharbour Farm team

Last autumn we sowed crimson clover on the 14-hectare north field and left the 12-hectare east field bare over winter. This summer the north field produced 8.1 tonnes of wheat per hectare, compared with 7.8 on the east field.

Our agronomist, Priya Nair, cautions that the north field has better drainage to begin with, so part of that gap may simply reflect soil conditions rather than the clover. She also notes that one season is not enough evidence to draw a conclusion. At this stage it is not yet clear whether the cover crop made any difference to yield. We will continue the trial next season to see whether the pattern holds.

**Cover Crop Trial: First-Season Summary**

Last autumn we sowed crimson clover as a cover crop on the 14-hectare north field and left the 12-hectare east field bare over winter, so the two fields would serve as a paired comparison.

This summer the north field produced 8.1 tonnes of wheat per hectare, compared with 7.8 on the east field. That is a 0.3 t/ha difference in favour of the clover field, but we want to be clear that we cannot yet attribute it to the cover crop.

Our agronomist, Priya Nair, has flagged two important caveats. First, the north field has better drainage than the east field, so part of the yield gap may simply reflect soil conditions rather than the clover. Second, a single season is not enough to draw a reliable conclusion; we will need to repeat the trial and control for field-to-field variation before we can say whether crimson clover is making a meaningful difference.

We will continue the trial next season and will share updated figures once we have a longer record. In the meantime, the result is best described as an early, inconclusive signal rather than evidence that the clover is responsible for the higher yield.

reply:
Cover Crop Trial Update

Last autumn we sowed crimson clover on the 14-hectare north field and left the 12-hectare east field bare over winter. This summer the north field yielded 8.1 tonnes of wheat per hectare, compared with 7.8 on the east field.

That is a difference of 0.3 tonnes per hectare, but we should not read too much into it yet. As our agronomist Priya Nair points out, the north field has better drainage to begin with, so part of the difference may be down to soil and ground conditions rather than the clover. One season is also not enough to judge. We will keep both fields under observation and look at the results again next year before drawing any conclusion about whether the crimson clover made a difference.

**Cover Crop Trial Update, Coldharbour Farm**

Last autumn we sowed crimson clover as a cover crop on the 14-hectare north field and left the 12-hectare east field bare over the winter. This summer the north field produced 8.1 tonnes of wheat per hectare, compared with 7.8 tonnes per hectare on the east field.

Our agronomist, Priya Nair, cautions that the north field has better drainage to begin with, so part of the difference may be attributable to underlying soil conditions rather than the clover. She also notes that a single growing season is too short a window to draw firm conclusions. On the evidence so far, it is not yet possible to say whether the crimson clover had a measurable effect on wheat yield. We will continue monitoring across further seasons before making any decisions about expanding the trial.

**Drip Irrigation Trial: First-Season Results**

This summer we fitted drip irrigation lines to 6 of our 20 beds to see how they would affect the tomato crop.

The tomato harvest from those 6 beds came in about 12 percent higher than last year. That is encouraging, but a few things are worth keeping in mind. This summer was cooler than usual, which can influence yields on its own. The beds that did not get drip lines also produced a little more than last year, so part of the overall increase may be due to the weather rather than the irrigation. And this is only one season of data, so it is too early to draw firm conclusions.

The committee will review the results next spring and decide whether to fit drip lines to the remaining beds. In the meantime, we will keep collecting data so we can make that call on a solid footing.
